subtitle: Right angles, parallel sides, equal sides, and the groups shapes share

traps.desc: counted how many shapes share the attribute instead of naming the shared number

problems.desc: (a) marked shapes, judged by eye: exactly the square and the rectangle should be circled, because those are the two shapes whose corners are all square corners. Circling the rhombus or the parallelogram, whose corners are not square corners, is not credit.

(b) instructor-judged. A full-credit answer says the square has four square corners so it belongs in the group, while the rhombus has four equal sides but its corners are not square corners, so equal sides alone do not put a shape in this group. An answer that only says the rhombus is tilted, or that repeats the shape names without naming the corner attribute, is not full credit.
problems.slot: (b) why a square belongs and a rhombus does not

problems.desc: (b) instructor-judged. A full-credit answer says a trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides and its corners are not all square corners, so it cannot join the four-square-corners group no matter how many sides it has. An answer that only says a trapezoid is a different shape, with no attribute named, is not full credit.
problems.slot: (b) why trapezoid tiles are not in that group

problems.key: at least one pair of parallel sides
problems.slot: (a) how many shapes are in the group

problems.desc: (b) instructor-judged. A full-credit answer says a shape belongs to every group whose attribute it has, and names two groups shape A really is in: four square corners, four equal sides, and two pairs of parallel sides are all true of it at once. Naming one group only, or saying a shape can belong to just one group, is not full credit.
problems.slot: (b) why one shape can be in two groups
